questions.stem: Wendy, 35, had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 8 days ago. She has not opened her bowels for 5 days, feels bloated and says her tummy looks bigger. You are taking her history in general practice. Which single question best helps tell simple constipation apart from postoperative ileus or bowel obstruction?
options: Have you noticed any bright red blood on the toilet paper?
Does your tummy feel bloated or look bigger than usual?
Are you still passing wind from your back passage?
How much water and fibre are you having each day?
questions.why: Passing flatus means the bowel is not completely obstructed and is moving, which argues against ileus or adhesive obstruction. After abdominal surgery, always ask about flatus, pain and vomiting before calling it simple constipation.
notes: Rectal bleeding points to a fissure or a colorectal cause, but it does not help separate constipation from ileus or obstruction.
Bloating and distension occur in both constipation and obstruction, so the answer does not tell them apart (and she has already told you this).
Fluid and fibre intake help explain why she is constipated, but they do not exclude an obstructed or paralysed bowel after surgery.

questions.stem: Wendy, 35, takes oxycodone 5 mg up to 4 times a day and daily oral iron after her cholecystectomy. She has hard pebbly stools, a loaded rectum and an acute anal fissure, with no features of obstruction. You plan to wean the oxycodone and start regular paracetamol. Which laxative regimen is most appropriate?
options: Psyllium 1 sachet twice daily, taken with extra water and a high-fibre diet
Macrogol 1 sachet once or twice daily plus senna 2 tablets at night
Docusate 120 mg twice daily as the only laxative, continued while on oxycodone
Subcutaneous methylnaltrexone 12 mg every second day, with no other laxative
questions.why: Opioid-induced constipation is treated with a regular osmotic and/or stimulant laxative, usually both (e.g. macrogol plus senna), adjusted to give a soft stool. The softer stool also lets her fissure heal.
notes: Bulk-forming laxatives are not recommended in opioid-induced constipation. They can make the stool harder or cause impaction when gut motility is slowed.
A stool softener used alone is weak and is not adequate for opioid-induced constipation; it does not overcome the slowed peristalsis.
Peripheral opioid antagonists are kept for constipation that fails standard laxatives, mostly in palliative care. They are not first line in a short opioid course.

questions.stem: Wendy, 35, has been taking oxycodone every day since her laparoscopic cholecystectomy 8 days ago. She now has hard, pellet-like stools that she has to strain to pass. Which mechanism best explains how the opioid causes her constipation?
options: Reduced bile acid delivery to the colon after cholecystectomy, which slows colonic transit
Muscarinic receptor blockade reducing parasympathetic drive to the colon and gut wall
A mainly central effect on transit that wears off as tolerance develops
Gut mu-receptor activation reduces propulsion and secretion, so more water is absorbed
questions.why: Opioids act on mu receptors in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. Propulsive peristalsis falls, non-propulsive tone rises, secretion falls and transit slows, so more water is absorbed and the stool becomes hard. Little tolerance develops to this gut effect.
notes: After cholecystectomy more bile acid reaches the colon, not less, and it tends to cause diarrhoea rather than constipation.
This is how anticholinergic drugs cause constipation. Opioids act through mu-opioid receptors.
Opioid constipation is mainly a peripheral enteric effect, and tolerance to it barely develops, which is why a laxative is needed for the whole course.

questions.stem: Anal inspection with a chaperone shows that Wendy, 35, has a posterior midline fissure in the anoderm below the dentate line. Passing a stool is very painful for her, and the DRE is uncomfortable. Which nerve carries the pain from this fissure?
options: Inferior rectal (anal) nerve, a branch of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4)
Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) via the inferior hypogastric plexus
Ilioinguinal nerve (L1), supplying skin of the anterior perineum
Sympathetic fibres from the sacral trunk via the superior rectal plexus
questions.why: Below the dentate line the anal canal has somatic sensory supply from the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve, so fissures there are sharply painful. Above the line the supply is visceral, so internal haemorrhoids are usually painless.
notes: Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry visceral afferents from above the dentate line. That mucosa is relatively insensitive to cutting or tearing.
The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the anterior labia or scrotum and the medial thigh, not the anal canal.
Sympathetic and visceral fibres serve the rectum and the upper anal canal. They do not carry the sharp somatic pain of a fissure below the dentate line.
